candidateRows: An all-loving God who desires relationship would make divine existence known to non-resistant people, yet religious belief remains strongly dependent on geography.
This establishes the principal evidential challenge to Christian theism by connecting divine love, relational availability, non-resistant unbelief, and demographic variation.
After the conversational setup, Joe formulates the hiddenness problem and develops geographic variation in belief as evidence that openness to God does not adequately explain unbelief.
Christianity need not dissolve divine hiddenness because its scriptures validate protest over God's absence and give believers grounds for treating that absence as genuinely troubling.
The move reframes the objection as an experience Christianity can recognize and ground, resisting the premise that a successful theistic response must eliminate the felt problem.
Joe's claim that an all-loving relational God should not remain hidden from non-resistant people.
Glen responds to the initial hiddenness case by appealing to biblical traditions of lament and arguing that a tidy balancing explanation would understate the seriousness of divine absence.
Divine hiddenness also afflicts committed believers and sincere adherents of rival faiths, so the problem concerns God's failure to sustain or clarify relationships as well as initial unbelief.
This broadens the hiddenness argument beyond atheists and makes resistance-based answers less sufficient by focusing on spiritually receptive believers and unresolved doctrinal disagreement.
Joe extends the discussion from non-resistant nonbelief to spiritual dryness, rival monotheistic faiths, and denominational disputes whose sincere participants receive no decisive divine correction.
Conscious existence, rational conversation, emotion, and participation in reality may already constitute a pervasive divine encounter rather than evidence that God is wholly absent.
It directly contests the experiential premise of hiddenness by redefining ordinary conscious and rational life as continuous participation in divine reality.
Joe's argument that sincere believers and nonbelievers are left without an adequate experience of God.
Glen answers the expanded hiddenness objection by asking whether the present exercise of consciousness, reason, rhetoric, and emotion should itself count as a profound experience of God.
God can be omnipresent yet personally encountered through incarnation, while human moral resistance can diminish awareness of divine nearness even among professing Christians.
The move supplies a distinctly Christian account of personal divine encounter and connects variations in experienced presence to morally significant resistance rather than simple divine absence.
Joe's concern that identifying all experience with God trivializes the personal and agential character central to theism.
After discussion of divine personality, Glen argues that the creator can enter creation personally and that failures to follow Jesus can reduce a believer's felt experience of God's nearness.

The noetic-effects-of-sin response cannot generally explain hiddenness because sinful believers still report faith, unbelief cannot non-circularly explain itself, and moral character does not closely track religious belief.
This directly challenges Glen's resistance explanation by identifying circularity, counterexamples, and the weak empirical association between moral conduct and perceived relationship with God.
Glen's proposal that resistance and failures to follow Jesus diminish people's experience of divine nearness.
Joe evaluates the claim that sin impairs knowledge of God, arguing that it cannot serve as a universal solution even if it contributes to a broader patchwork of explanations.

Historically inherited impairment of an intuitive sense of God does not resolve hiddenness, because an all-loving God could intervene when a person becomes responsible and offer a genuine opportunity to respond.
The move concedes cultural contingency while arguing that divine love should overcome undeserved epistemic disadvantage at the point of personal responsibility, preserving the central objection.
Glen's account of historically contingent intellectual error and culturally ingrained dispositions that can lead people away from divine truth.
Joe grants that inherited culture may weaken intuitive awareness of God but argues that this is not the individual's fault and should prompt timely divine outreach rather than continued silence.
The crucified and God-forsaken Christ does not remove every hiddenness problem but reveals a God who enters humanity's abandonment and thereby makes Christian trust possible amid divine absence.

This is the principal Christological answer in the chunk, claiming that Christianity uniquely grounds the seriousness of hiddenness while portraying God as sharing the condition that generates the objection.
Joe's contention that an all-loving God should intervene for people whose cultural circumstances leave them unable to perceive God.

Glen portrays humanity as entangled in personal and structural evil, then presents the crucifixion as divine participation in abandonment and as the basis for trust without claiming a complete solution.

Nonbelievers may relate unknowingly to God through their experience of goodness, but a complete hiddenness solution would also require salvation to remain open without explicit Christian belief or gospel access.
The proposal offers a substantive route around propositional hiddenness while exposing its necessary theological cost: inclusivism about relationship with God and ultimate salvation.
Joe suggests that experiencing goodness may constitute an unrecognized relationship with its divine source, then argues that this account must be paired with an inclusivist view of salvation.
The force of the problem of evil is best grasped through concrete cases of apparently gratuitous suffering, where appeals to soul-making or a higher plan become difficult to credit.
This opens the debate's second major challenge to Christian theism and identifies apparently pointless innocent suffering as the evidential burden that theistic explanations must meet.
After the transition from hiddenness to evil, Joe argues that gruesome examples such as a blameless child's death preserve the objection's moral force better than abstract calculations.
The Christian account of Job culminates in Christ, who bears creation's suffering and uniquely judges its ultimate cost worthwhile in light of resurrection.
This directly advances the Christian explanation of evil by connecting human epistemic limits, divine participation in suffering, and resurrection hope.
Joe Folley's claim that Job supports accepting our inability to understand God's reasons for permitting evil.
After Joe appeals to Job and human finitude, Glen develops Job as a scriptural pattern completed by Christ's suffering and resurrection.
Skeptical theism can answer hiddenness and evil only at the cost of weakening other theistic arguments that require intelligible divine motives.
The argument identifies an internal tradeoff for Christian theism: divine inscrutability protects against objections while undermining moral grounding and fine-tuning reasoning.
Glen Scrivener's appeal to Job and Christ as grounds for trusting divine judgment despite apparently inscrutable suffering.
Joe first notes that the proposed answers presuppose belief, then argues that excessive divine inscrutability destabilizes affirmative arguments for God.
A genuine problem of evil depends on objective moral grounding, and theism supplies the personal and normative authority needed to condemn evil rather than merely accept it.
This reverses the problem of evil into an argument for theism by claiming that moral indignation itself requires a transcendent standard.
Joe Folley's contention that Christian answers to evil are conditional on a prior commitment to God's existence.
Following discussion of divine comprehensibility, Glen argues that condemning suffering as genuinely evil may itself require a theistic moral framework.
The problem of evil can operate as an internal Christian critique, although a personal divine commander may give moral realism greater motivational force than impersonal Platonism.
The move preserves the force of the evil objection without external moral assumptions while granting a significant practical advantage to personal theistic morality.
Glen Scrivener's argument that one needs something like theism to sustain a morally serious problem of evil.
Joe distinguishes an internal inconsistency objection from external moral grounding, then explains why divine commands can motivate more readily than abstract goodness.
Grounding moral motivation in God's enforceable power risks reducing obedience to coercion, while grounding it in goodness alone leaves unclear what God adds to an impersonal good.
This presents a dilemma for theistic moral grounding between morally empty divine power and a motivational role already available to independent goodness.
The preceding claim that a personal divine commander improves on an impersonal Platonic form by authoritatively enforcing morality.
After acknowledging theism's motivational advantage, Joe tests its limits through a coercive divine-command example and formulates a two-sided tension.
The Trinity answers the Euthyphro dilemma because eternal other-centered divine love is neither an external standard nor an arbitrary command but goodness itself.
The argument supplies Christianity's central proposed foundation for objective morality while addressing both arbitrariness and motivationally empty abstraction.
Joe Folley's dilemma between coercive divine power and an independently existing goodness that apparently makes God unnecessary.
Glen reframes divine goodness through the eternal interpersonal life of the Trinity and contrasts this personal foundation with Platonic abstraction.
Every moral system must bridge descriptive goodness to normative motivation, and theism faces this gap too, though its interpersonal commands may bridge it more easily.
This qualifies the proposed Trinitarian solution by distinguishing goodness from obligation while conceding a comparative motivational advantage to theism.
Glen Scrivener's proposal that Trinitarian divine love personally grounds goodness and avoids the Euthyphro dilemma.
Joe argues that identifying goodness still does not automatically generate obligation, but accepts that a personal relation with God narrows the motivational gap.
Naturalism cannot adequately call suffering objectively wrong, whereas Christian theism grounds moral condemnation in an objective standard of goodness.
This directly compares the rival worldviews on objective moral value and turns the moral response to suffering into positive support for Christianity.
As the discussion shifts to morality, Glen contrasts naturalistic indifference with the Christian ability to condemn suffering as objectively evil.
Moral anti-realism can make moral judgments inherently motivating through their emotive content, whereas any purely propositional realism faces a gap between recognizing good and caring about it.
The move offers a substantive non-theistic alternative for explaining moral motivation and identifies a general weakness in realist moral theories.
Glen Scrivener's claim that naturalism lacks the resources to identify suffering as objectively and motivationally significant evil.
Joe considers a constructivist route but emphasizes the motivational gap, arguing that emotive moral states connect judgment with action more directly.
Theism is one route to moral realism but not the only one, and much apparent contemporary moral disagreement is actually disagreement about descriptive facts rather than basic values.
This resists the claim that objective morality uniquely supports theism and explains substantial moral convergence without requiring a shared religious foundation.
Glen Scrivener's objection that emotivism cannot classify approval of murder as objectively mistaken or morally wrong.
Joe grants anti-realism's limitation, allows that theism can support realism, but argues for alternative epistemic routes and extensive agreement on underlying values.
Modern secular human-rights discourse retains Christian assumptions about human dignity while materialism cannot adequately sustain those assumptions.
This directly supports Christian theism's comparative account of morality by arguing that secular moral language depends upon inherited theological concepts.
The earlier account that religious narratives motivate morality without establishing that their moral content is uniquely true.
After agreement that humans need moral narratives, the speaker connects souls, human rights, and equality to Christian inheritance and contrasts that inheritance with modern materialism.
Moral values spread through shared sacred narratives, but the movement from theological propositions to later moral conclusions is loose and historically evolutionary.
The move grants religion's motivational power while challenging any simple logical derivation of moral progress from fixed Christian doctrine.
The earlier claim that secular human valuation and rights discourse are layered expressions of an underlying Christian moral framework.
The speaker explains why values seek shared justification, why narratives unify moral communities, and why Christianity's historical moral development is not straightforward deduction.
An apologetic appeal to Christian moral development requires advance criteria distinguishing genuine doctrinal flowerings from corruptions.
This challenges the explanatory force of Christian moral progress by arguing that hindsight alone cannot identify which historical developments authentically follow Christianity.
The earlier presentation of Christian ideas and narratives as the inherited source from which modern moral equality and rights developed.
Abolition, persecution, and universalism illustrate that rival developments can claim Christian roots, creating a need for non-retrospective standards of authenticity.
Christian moral development can be judged rather than merely retrofitted because scripture stands above historical Christendom and can condemn its deviations.
The move supplies a proposed Christian standard for separating authentic development from corruption, answering a central objection to the Dominion-style account.
The challenge that Christianity needs criteria independent of hindsight to distinguish doctrinal development from corruption.
The speaker notes recognition of genuinely post-Christian developments, rejects treating every Western change as Christian, and proposes scripture as a judgment over the church.
A realist account of moral progress must preserve eternal truths while explaining discovery over time and must identify prospective checks on both progress and regression.
This presses a fundamental tension in the Christian realist explanation of moral progress and demands a method capable of identifying future advances and errors.
The proposed use of scripture to judge historical Christianity and distinguish legitimate moral development from deviation.
The speaker contrasts timeless moral truth with gradual human discovery, warns against retrospective fitting, and argues that a flowering metaphor cannot perform the needed analysis.
Scripture itself depicts patient, directed moral development in which God regulates nonideal conditions while restoring humanity toward a prior moral ideal.
This offers the positive Christian mechanism requested by the opposing side: historically patient accommodation governed by a scriptural narrative and moral destination.
The objection that moral realism needs more than a flowering metaphor to explain change and identify genuine moral development.
Divorce legislation, Jesus's appeal to creation, kingdom-growth imagery, and the nonfinal status of modern rights instruments form a directed biblical account of development.
New historical and technological shocks expose further applications of ancient Christian truths, with the image of God remaining indispensable for future questions about humanity.
The move extends the proposed Christian model prospectively, claiming it can guide future moral development rather than merely redescribe past changes.
The question whether eternal moral truth still contains aspects awaiting discovery through future historical circumstances.
The speaker uses slavery and technological disruption as examples of contingent pressures that reveal applications of enduring doctrine while allowing both advances and reversals.
The controlling test for Christian moral development is conformity to scripture's Jesus-centered narrative of self-giving, world-embracing forgiveness.
This provides the speaker's clearest concrete criterion for judging purported Christian progress or regression, resolving the debate's repeated methodological challenge.
The objection that Christians need to know when apparent developments are actually backward steps undertaken in Jesus's name.
Rather than isolated proof texts or an abstract synthesis, the speaker centers judgment on the scriptural narrative culminating in the crucified and forgiving Jesus.
Moral emotion remains indispensable even for cognitivists who affirm moral truth, so anti-realist insights should not be discarded wholesale.
The move qualifies the realism-versus-anti-realism contrast by preserving emotion's motivational role within an account that still recognizes moral truth.
The preceding appeal to an emotionally powerful Jesus-centered test and the speaker's joking description of it as emotivist.
The speaker treats affective moral response as compatible with cognitivism and argues that accepting moral truths need not eliminate useful anti-realist insights.
Embodied Christian practices continually nourish moral progress by immersing communities in the self-giving narrative of Jesus despite inevitable wrong turns.
This returns the discussion to Christianity's practical motivational advantage, explaining how its narrative is enacted communally rather than held only as propositions.
The preceding claim that moral emotion remains important even within a cognitivist account of objective moral truth.
The church's images, shared table, music, and peace-making practices embody the Jesus story, which the speaker expects to sustain progress through historical complexity.
